title: An honest and good heart (Luke 8:4–21)
hook: the good soil keeps the word and bears fruit with patience

segments.voice: Yesterday, the women who paid: Mary Magdalene, Joanna, Susanna and many others. Your line was the women paid. Who did you thank for their quiet work? Day five hundred thirty-one.

A tomato seed goes into the ground. You water it and check it the next morning. Nothing. Check it again. Nothing. A week later, a thin green thread. Weeks after that, maybe, something red. The waiting is the hard part. A huge crowd has gathered from town after town, and Jesus tells them a story about exactly that. "A sower went out to sow his seed." Some of it lands on the path and gets trampled and eaten by birds. Some on rock, where it sprouts and withers for lack of moisture. Some among thorns that choke it. And some on good ground, where it grows and bears a hundredfold.

Jesus explains: "The seed is the word of God." The path is people who hear, but the word is snatched away before it settles. The rock is people who receive it with joy, but have no root, and fall away when testing comes. The thorns are people choked by "cares and riches and pleasures of this life." Then the good ground, with two details worth slowing down for. In the King James words: "But that on the good ground are they, which in an honest and good heart, having heard the word, keep it, and bring forth fruit with patience." An honest and good heart. In Greek, kale kai agathe, a pairing some scholars say Greek writers used for a noble, upright person. Here it describes the heart the good soil stands for. And with patience. The Greek is hupomone, endurance; some readers unpack it as remaining under, staying put under a weight. The good soil isn't the soil where things happen fast. It's the soil that holds on through the season. Then two short sayings. A lamp isn't lit to be put under a bed. And: "Take heed therefore how ye hear." Not just what you hear: how. Finally, Jesus' mother and brothers arrive and can't reach him through the crowd. Someone tells him, and he answers: "My mother and my brethren are these which hear the word of God, and do it." Some readers take that not as pushing his family away but as widening the circle; Luke has already shown Mary keeping words in her heart. Hear and keep. Keep and do. Do, and wait. That's the whole chapter's rhythm.
screen: `THE SEED IS THE WORD OF GOD.`
then, large: `KEEP IT, AND BRING FORTH FRUIT WITH PATIENCE.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: be patient with slow fruit. Settle, and breathe. Think of something in your life that's growing slowly, maybe so slowly you've started to doubt it's growing at all. A child's character. A friendship you're rebuilding. A garden, a neighborhood, someone else's recovery. Picture it as a seed in the ground in late winter. You can't see what's happening below the surface, and the not-seeing is part of the process. Breathe in, and remember: remaining under. Breathe out, and let go of the need to see results today. Let your attention rest on the soil itself, the steady, honest work of staying. If you pray, you can ask for patience with slow things. If you don't, simply rest with the waiting. The bell holds the time.
Hupomone, Luke's Greek word for patience, endurance, staying under a weight: in the parable of the sower, the good soil is people who hear the word, keep it, and bear fruit with patience.
Your line: bear fruit with patience. Today, when something you care about seems stuck, water it once more and leave it alone. Day five hundred thirty-one.

howItsDone: The parable of the sower is often read in churches and used in Christian teaching as a way to reflect on how people hear and keep scripture over time.

fork.setup: you've planted good seed. weeks pass and nothing shows. what does Luke's good soil do?
options: keep it, and bring forth fruit with patience.
fork.reveal: the good ground keeps the word and bears fruit with patience: hupomone, remaining under, holding on through the season.

original.note: Greek: patience, endurance. often explained as remaining under, staying put beneath a load.

trapdoor: what you thought: some people are good soil and some aren't.
what it means: the good soil is a heart that hears, keeps and stays, bearing fruit slowly, with patience.
what a scholar hears: "honest and good," kale kai agathe, echoes a Greek pairing for an upright, noble person, here used of the heart the good soil stands for.

notes: kalos kai agathos (kalokagathia) as a Greek ideal of the noble person: common scholarly note. Confirm the Greek of 8:15 (en kardia kale kai agathe).
hupomone 'remaining under' (hupo + meno): standard lexicon etymology.
Day 531 is outside week boundaries; 532 is the week end.
Jesus' brothers: Catholic and Orthodox Christians understand 'brethren' as relatives or step-brothers; the script quotes the verse without comment. Keeper may want a note.
